extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers seeking representation from literary agents
extracted.subtask_description: Create a tight, well-rehearsed 30-second (or shorter) pitch to present to a literary agent in person that states who you are, what you want, why you're the best choice, and includes a clear call to action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevator pitch length (30 seconds or fewer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to pitch your idea in 30 seconds or fewer (this is called an 'Elevator Pitch').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the pitch tight and time-limited so you never waste an opportunity. Cultivate a well-rehearsed sound-byte pitch and commit a few key sentences to memory. The page offers a free download, 'Your 30-Second Pitch,' for further tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the literary agent who you are
rubrics_metrics.description: State your name and job title, or the title of the position you're seeking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a clear self-introduction. Example: 'Hi, my name is Miranda Mechanic, and I’m a licensed automotive mechanic who writes how-to articles for women who don’t want their cars to get the best of them.' Keep it brief and directly relevant to what you're pitching.

rubrics_metrics.name: State what you want (be direct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the literary agent what you are after; don’t beat around the bush.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Say plainly what you want (representation, placement, a meeting, etc.). Example: 'I’m interested in placing some of my articles with your magazine, Auto Care for Everybody.' Avoid vagueness or hedging; direct requests increase chances of follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show why you’re the best choice (relevant qualifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: List degrees, writing credentials, training, or experience that relate to your stated goal and show why you’re a good fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give qualifications that match the stated goal; be brief and memorable. Example: 'I’ve been taking mechanical things apart since before I could walk, and I’m the owner-operator of my own body shop.' Do not list unrelated credentials (anti-pattern: saying you want to write on mechanics but citing degrees in early Russian literature). If you lack directly related experience, name transferable qualities or skills such as attention to detail or passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a clear call to action
rubrics_metrics.description: End the pitch by asking for the next step or what you want the agent to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A call to action leads to further interaction; explicitly ask to show work, set up a meeting, or exchange contact info. Example: 'I’d like to show you copies of my articles, including “How to Change a Tire When It’s Twenty Below Zero” and “How to Add Oil When You’re Wearing a Power Suit.”' Don’t neglect this step—selling yourself without asking for something wastes the opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor the pitch to agent type and market
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt your pitch to the agent’s market, specialty, and location (e.g., New York vs. London, children’s vs. Christian, top-ranking vs. new agents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a few key sentences that work across different types of agents but be ready to tweak emphasis or examples depending on the agent’s focus. The page stresses the same basic structure applies whether pitching to varied agent types, but specifics should match the agent’s interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be brief, memorable, and rehearsed
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive for a pitch that is concise, distinctive, and practiced so it can be delivered smoothly in a short encounter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commit the pitch to memory and rehearse so it sounds natural and confident. Focus on 'that special something that separates you from the crowd.' Aim for a memorable hook or unique angle rather than long lists of facts.
